utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, assisted by Crispian Smith, Case Manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cukic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic, I'm reminded that the -- inasmuch -- notwithstanding that it would have been alerted to the Chamber by the Zupljanin Defence team last week about his absence every day this week that it is necessary for the record for counsel to indicate each day that he is not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Zupljanin is not appearing today. He sent a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before the witness -- before examination-in-chief continues, we had undertaken yesterday to rule this morning on the application for the admission into evidence of the last document to which the witness spoke. Whereas, on the face of it, there appears to be some connection between the -- the -- the witness is able to speak somehow to the contents of the document, which may argue for its become marked for identification. We're not satisfied that it is -- that it could be admitted through this witness because the answers that the witness has given in terms of the document and its -- his familiarity with it is simply to remote from him. So it may be admissible through another witness, but at this stage we rule that it should not be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- as I say, it's not one where I'm going to start arguing again, but it's unlikely - can I put it this way; no harm in that - that we're likely to have another witness who can speak to the contents at all. So, I mean, it really depends whether or not the question of how the judicial system came to be into being in the Republika Srpska is a matter which Your Honours consider is relevant to the case. I mean, it may well be that we'll have to return to this at a later stage when we're clearly going to have to apply for some documents to come in through bar table motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is what I'm thinking, so perhaps it could be -- so that we don't lose it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- it should be marked for identification at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'm happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can we continue then, please --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be marked as Exhibit P1324, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mandic, before Ms. Korner continues, I remind you that you're still on your oath. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, as you appreciate, I'm taking you through documents in what I hope is a chronological order and documents that you haven't been asked to talk about in your previous testimony. So could have you a look, please, first of all, at document P427.16.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, tab, sorry. 58.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, this is a document addressed to the -- from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's dated the 15th of May, and it's signed "Government Secretary, Nedeljko Lakic." Did you know Mr. Lakic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was Mr. Lakic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the secretary in the government of Mr. Djeric, where I was a minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was he the person who actually took the minutes of the government meetings, a couple of which we're going to look at?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he may have been, but he didn't have to. The government secretary has certain responsibilities that were prescribed by a piece of legislation, governing the work of the government. He may have taken minutes but not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But what I want to ask you about is it's dated the 15th of May and it's addressed to the Crisis Staff in Ilijas. It says: "Please approve and provide passage through your territory for the group of prisoners who are presently at Pale and travelling to Viseko." "Transport and escort for these prisoners will be provided by the Crisis Staff of Pale. "Please destroy that approval the moment when the prisoners leave Ilijas municipality." Now, this is at a period about four days before you were officially appointed to be minister of justice, but you told us that you already knew that were going to be. Why was that approval to be destroyed when the prisoners left?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the government secretary did not have authority to send such letters. It's not within his purview. Now, on what basis and on whose orders he did this, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Ministry of Justice was in charge, wasn't it, of the -- of the prisons. And, as we'll see, you had something to do -- well, we've already talked about the exchange of prisoners. Now, did you have anything to do with this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With this letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as you say, the government secretary was hardly likely to send this on his own authority, was he? Who would have given him the authority to send this letter?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he either did it on his own initiative or on the orders of the prime minister, because he was responsible only to the prime minister. And this is quite outside the system. It's some sort of private letter. It never passed through the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, do you know what "prisoners in Pale" refers to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave that, then, please, and can we move, as I say, to other matters concerning prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at P179.17, which is tab 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, before you move on. Mr. Mandic, do I understand from your answers about this last document that was shown to you by counsel that because, on the face of it, it's irregular for the reasons that you have given that it may not be authentic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not doubting its authenticity. I'm not saying that Nedeljko Lakic did not sign it, but it's irregular. The government secretary is an administrative employee who takes care of the work of the government within the cabinet itself, within the ministries. He has no outside authority. It's the ministries who act on the outside in the field. The secretary of the government is a technical staff member. He has no authority to give any instructions to any municipalities, be it Pale or Ilijas, to do anything. He has no authority, and it's an irregular letter. It must have been some private connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think some light's going to be shone on it by this document, Your Honours, on this previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, I didn't get that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think will you see some light is going to be shed on that document we just looked at by this document that we're about to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Mandic, this document is headed, is it not: The total of 400 persons, who were driven from Bratunac to Pale, are listed on 18 pages. And if you go to the next page -- third page, I think, in each.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, third page in each.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's dated the -- well, in the translation it's got the 14th of May. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's -- says in handwriting, as we can see, there are 400 persons, member of the government's commission on behalf of the Serbian MUP for the exchange of prisoners of war, Slobodan Markovic. Did you know Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Never heard of him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then it's a list, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we just go to the -- page -- two pages on; page 5 in English and probably the same in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a list of people, all of whom, on the face of it, are Muslims from Bratunac. Do you agree with that, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware - I mean, you were based in Pale at this stage, weren't you? - that 400 people had been brought from Bratunac to Pale and would have seen to have been transferred for the purposes of exchange?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm seeing this list for the first time, and I did not know that some people were brought from Bratunac to Pale. I don't know who brought them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you -- before you took up your appointment as minister of justice, was anybody else acting as minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ministry of Justice, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think so. Ranko Nikolic had been appointed minister of justice. We discussed this yesterday. That was in December or perhaps January 1992. He failed to show up to take up his new post, and before April I was informed at a meeting of a body called Security Council or something like that, that I would be taking over the Ministry of Justice, because the minister of justice, Ranko Nikolic, did not show up for work. I believe I was the first one to occupy that position. Whether anyone from the joint Ministry of Justice had been transferred already to the Ministry of Justice and had already started working, I don't know, because yesterday's document dated 1st May indicates that some people had been working at the Ministry of Justice before I arrived, because until the beginning of May, I was at Vrace, at the school in Vrace; that's where I was based. I was not in Pale. I was in Vrace, standing in for Mico Stanisic, whereas Mico Stanisic was at Pale at the headquarters of the MUP of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is what I want to ask you about. Until such time as there was a functioning Ministry of Justice when you took over, who was in charge of matters such as prisons and prisoners? Which organ -- which ministry?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no ministry in charge of it, and it was not decided at the level of the government. Every Crisis Staff, every municipality, every region had its own Crisis Staff and its own commission for prisoners. It was at the local level. The Serb state had not started to operate properly, and it was later only that the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War was formed later for Republika Srpska, and it's established by a series of documents. There were regions and autonomous regions before that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can I just say something. As you know, because we have the [indiscernible], we have a limited amount of time, we have a number of documents to get through, so if you could simply concentrate and answer on the question I asked. If more explanation is needed, I'll ask you for it. Are you saying, therefore, that in the beginning of May before you took up your appointment there was no ministry actually in charge of prisoners but the regions and the local Crisis Staffs dealt with prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From all I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of Interior have anything to do with this, the prisoners, and the transfer of them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you were still in -- in -- until May the 19th, the assistant minister for the police; acting, if you like. So don't you know whether or not the Ministry of Interior had responsibilities for prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on then, please. Can we look next, please, at -- a record of an intercept between you and somebody else. I think we'll find it's Karisik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, it's document 1319; tab 60. I'm sorry, P179.17.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, the previous document was tab 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it? Oh, so it was. Tab 61. So sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. It's still 32 -- it's document -- it's 65 ter 3249. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a -- apparently a conversation between you and somebody called Milena. You're trying to get hold of General Mladic. And if we go to the second page -- no, second page, you're leaving a message saying that you were calling from the barracks in Lukavica. And at what stage in May - because we don't have an accurate date - were you in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there all the time at Vrace and Lukavica. It's one and the same place, in the Serbian territory. That barracks was about 1 kilometre away from the school at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say then - can we go to the third page - you are saying that General Mladic should call you urgently. You say: "Some security chap has arrived, Boskovic from Belgrade. They want to let the cadets go without weapons but to leave the weapons to these Turks despite the agreement and the plans of our government and General Mladic." What were you referring to there? Shortly, please, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two or three barracks, one of them was the Marsal Tito barracks, and they were all surrounded by the Territorial Defence or other members of the Muslim ethnicity. Inside were cadets, conscripts, aged 16 and 17, and the Muslim Territorial Defence didn't want to let them out. And this man from the security forces came from Belgrade to get them out of the barracks peacefully, but the Muslim side imposed a condition that all the weapons be left inside the barracks. I wanted to inform the competent authorities, so I called Djeric, the prime minister, Karadzic, the president of the state, and Krajisnik -- sorry, Mladic, from the army, to let them know. I was still with the police at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is before the 19th of May then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was right at the beginning of May or even the end of April. I don't know when these children were evacuated from the barracks, because their water supply, their electricity supply had been cut off. They had no food. They were in a very difficult position. They were cadets, students, at this military school in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... intervention in the transcript. Page 10, line 18. It says the "preliminary" side. I believe he said the "Muslim" side imposed a condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he did. I heard that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm now in French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then can we very quickly have a look, please, at another record of a conversation that you had, this time with Mr. Prstojevic, which is document number 3256, tab 63.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that these were all given numbers yesterday, but I have no idea what the numbers are, so I'm just referring to them by 65 ter -- I mean, exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we've now moved to the 2nd of June. Who is -- can you just tell the Court, remind the Court, who Mr. Prstojevic was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Prstojevic was the head of the Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you're speaking to him --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at page 3 in English, and it's page 3 also in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You ask him at the top of the page whether there are any problems. And there's a discussion about where he comes from and what Mr. Prstojevic does. And then you say this: "It has come to our attention and that of the government that you are issuing ultimatums to some Turks, evicting people from certain settlements, and people respond badly to it. They are abusing this, those Muslims and the media and so on." And he says: "Yes." And you say: "Please do not do anything like this. Consult with Djeric first and those people up there, because this is very bad publicity for us and for everyone. They have the civil option; they are killing and expelling us. They have to be a little more flexible there ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we go over the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... and not touch those Muslims who are willing to listen and who are loyal. We cannot ethnically cleanse Ilidza or any other place. At least that is the attitude of the government and the political leadership and all. It has already reached the top how in some settlement you gave them 24 hours to move out ..." Now, stopping there for a moment. Why were you make this phone call to Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called him because, before me, Tomo Kovac made a call, who was the chief of police, and he complained to me about Prstojevic's blocking the whole of Ilidza and expelling the non-Serb populations. Since I knew him personally, I called him and I told him that everyone, including Mr. Djeric, was against that, that we shouldn't -- that he shouldn't touch these people, that he should let them go. We had a problem with Fadil Musanovic, who was a misdemeanor judge who wanted to do his work. However, he expelled him from his job. I insisted on him being reinstated in his position, that this was no way how things should be done, this was not in the spirit of how Serbs operate, and it was contrary to the Geneva Conventions. Because those people were not guilty of anything. In mild terms, I tried to persuade him not to do what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But Mr. Tomo Kovac, the chief of police, had informed me before that about what he was doing, and that was very bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll see, if we go on, we'll see what you then say. Mr. Prstojevic says, well, effectively: "We did say that, not in public." And you say: "I know what it should be and how we should operate." And he insists: "We didn't say it in public, nor did we write it down." And then you say this: "Please, in this context, you know what is necessary. You are ... probably up there during the talks ... and how it should be done and those Muslims who said that about us ... this has to be some sort of protection." And there you refer to the judge you've just spoken about. "In that context, Fadil Musanovic is a judge. But, look, talk to him. If he has not already fled, place him to work for us so that we can say that we employ everyone, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, regardless of nationality as long as they are loyal to the Serbian state. So have a look, please, place two or three Muslims somewhere ..." So, Mr. Mandic, were you saying there that, effectively, you need to be able to say to the international community that everybody was employed by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some people who thought that only Serbs should be filling certain positions. As I said, in a mild terms and in a political way I tried to persuade him to leave the non-Serbs where they lived and where they worked. I didn't dare and I couldn't use any stronger terms, because I didn't have any competence to do that. Rather, I resorted to a mild political persuasion with a view to making him keep those people in their places. There were many of such people in those smaller regions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you get the feeling that not everybody who was part of the creation of the Serbian state realised, as you did, that it was important that the international community should believe that everyone was able to live within the Serbian state and be employed by them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there were individuals who thought that only Serbs should live in this Serbian state. I don't think there were too many of such people like Prstojevic was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just ask why you used the expression in this element: "... place him to work for us so that we can say that we employ everyone." Say to whom that you employ everyone?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the media outlets, Mr. Izetbegovic advocated for a civilian state, and he kept insisting that all structures should be made up of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. So I followed the same line and I said that we should behave in the same manner that we, in other words, have both Serbs and non-Serbs working and living there. That seems to me to be only normal and logical because Bosnia-Herzegovina was a mixture of ethnicities and you couldn't separate people, especially and particularly along political lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I believe page 14, line 15, when it starts "Because ..." should be marked as an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's the answer by the witness, and it's recorded as your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, please, on this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look, please, at the next page in English and I -- yes, I think the next page in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic says -- he's effectively talking about Hrasnica and Sokolac and releasing Serbs. And then he says: "Our misdemeanour court did not receive a single report. No one submitted any." And you say: "Well, push Tomo Kovac and the police. Make them work. They're looting there, disrupting public peace and order." Firstly, when you say "looting there, disrupting public peace and order," is that the police you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the population, since Kovac was chief of police, I was asking Mr. Prstojevic to enforce the police to engage the police officers to prevent any disturbance of public law and order and to prevent looting and that they should bring in the offenders, because you see I say that there were gangs of thieves, war profiteers, et cetera, and the police should do their job and arrest them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Mandic, that's all I want to ask you on that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move now, please, to document 2562, which is tab 64.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is dated a few days after the conversation that you've just had. It's 5th of June, and it's addressed to the Ministry of Justice, and it's the delivery of the proposal of candidates for the judicial bodies in Bijeljina. And we see that various proposals are made. Did you get this document in your capacity by then, definitely as minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we can see that the 18 candidates are proposed as judges. Can you indicate which of those, as far as you're aware, are non-Serbs, were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my letter, I had asked that the positions of both judges and prosecutors be filled by people from all ethnic groups. You can see here Cviko Adamovic is a Muslim; Vujic, Zivko is a Croat; Diko Pajkanovic, a Muslim; Alma Salihbegovic, a Muslim; Alida Nadj-Madjarac, Muslim; Gruhonjic Muhamed, a Muslim; and they were all appointed judges in the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, that's the next question I want to ask you. The system was, wasn't it, that the Assembly had to ratify the appointments, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was based on my proposal that the Assembly made these assignments. And these appointments were public in the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska. Not only from the area of Bijeljina, but other Serb-held territories, like Trebinje, Banja Luka, et cetera. As far as the ethnic composition is concerned, the Ministry of Justice completely reflected the composition of the population living in those areas. And we insisted on that from day one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I want to ask you, please, is it your testimony that all of these proposal for Bijeljina, the appointments, were made by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. First President Karadzic signed their appointments according to the constitution, and then it was transferred to the Assembly to formerly confirm their appointments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, would Your Honours just give me one moment. As usual, I've just lost ... a document I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The appointments were published, you say, in the gazette. Is that right, the Official Gazette of the Serbian People?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just ask you this: Are you sure that, for example, a leader - I can't pronounce her name, I'm afraid - Nadj-Madjarac was appointed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dozens and dozens of judges and prosecutors of all nationalities were appointed. Whether Alida had left in the meantime and was not appointed, I cannot be positive. But can you see for yourself, if you check the Official Gazette, that many people, non-Serbs, that is to say, Croats and Muslims, were appointed to all kinds of posts in the Ministry of Judiciary of Republika Srpska during my term of office. Whether Alida particularly was appointed, I don't remember. I don't remember even some other names. But I'm quite sure that these were the candidates and that their names, on behalf of the Ministry of Justice, were given and passed on as our proposals. I think that Alida only was re-appointed, but maybe she left in the meantime. I have no particular details about any specific case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just so that you understand, I'm not suggesting that you didn't put these people forward at all. What I'm asking you now, and we're going to look at the Banja Luka ones in a little more detail, is whether you are able to tell us whether, either that lady or indeed Mr. Gruhonjic Muhamed, the Assembly actually approved those appointments?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can categorically assert that all my proposals were endorsed by the Assembly and Dr. Radovan Karadzic. If some of those persons left Republika Srpska, went to the Federation, or went abroad, which happened, then most probably if they were absent their appointments were not confirmed. But as far as my proposals are concerned, relating to non-Serbs, none of my proposals had ever been rejected by either Dr. Karadzic or the Assembly. I am positive on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- solely based on the grounds that they were a Muslim or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay. We'll leave that topic for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1325, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we next, please, look at, very briefly, at the minutes of the government for the 10th of June, which is P260 -- oh, no, sorry, it's not. It's P179.7.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, minutes of the 10th of June. You and Mico Stanisic are both there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go, please, in English to the third page; and in B/C/S, it's the second page, under Agenda item 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see there that the Ministry of Justice should make a report about prisoners. The report should pay special attention on the treatment of the civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera, and the report would be considered by the government, after which it would be submitted to the Presidency. Now, did that arise because there had been complaints about the treatment of the civilian population in particular?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And -- and -- and where -- who had been making the complaints?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government received information to that effect, either through the police or the municipal authorities or individuals from municipalities. Because at one point all the municipalities started acting like mini states, and they established their mini prisons. In the process of creating Republika Srpska and the authority, an attempt was made to centralise this and to have all the prisons and all the reception facilities be governed by law and by the international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You spoke about this, Mr. Mandic, thank you, in your previous testimony. So I don't need take that any further. All right, thank you. That's all --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... about that. Let me just check ... Yes. Because I think we see the results of this. Could you have a look, please, at document ... P427.11. Now, this is the meeting held five days after the last one. You actually weren't present, but you sent Mr. -- is it Lale, Vojin Lale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojin Lale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go, please, in this one, to the fourth page in English; and in -- it's also the fourth page in B/C/S, Agenda item 10. In fact -- I suppose we should have looked at the second page -- sorry, can we just go to the second page first, because we need to see what Agenda item 10 was. Second page in each. Agenda item 10 was the -- a report and proposed measures for improving the work of the Central Committee for an exchange of prisoners of war, detained persons, and bodies of killed persons that are left behind the enemy lines. And then, if we go back to where I originally was, discussion of Agenda 10 on the fourth page. The government has considered the proposed report. It's been concluded that the issue of prisoners exchange is extremely important, complex, and delicate, and that if sufficient attention is not paid to it, it can cause a number of negative consequences for the whole republic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know you weren't there, Mr. Mandic, but I assume Mr. Lale reported to you. What was it that might cause negative consequences?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we were receiving bad news about ill-treatment of detained people in individual municipalities, the government decided to set up a very strong group, consisting of the Prime Minister Djeric; Milan Trbojevic; Dragan Kalinic, health minister; Mico Stanisic, chief of police; Bogdan Subotic, defence minister; and myself as the minister of justice in order to consider all these problems and find quick solutions. That was a major problem for Republika Srpska and also for the people who were held in municipal detention units and prisons. That had to be given immediate attention and solved. And since this commission was not able to resolve this issue, we had to include and involve the highest officials in order to prevent any unlawful arrests and detention of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Mandic. That's all I want to ask you about that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move, now, to document number 70, please -- sorry, 1D95, once we've correlated Defence exhibits with ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is apparently a report by somebody called Dr. Nikola Poplasen. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know Dr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it says he was a commissioner at the republic level. What exactly was his job?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of Republika Srpska appointed him to govern the municipality of Vogosca and to disband the Crisis Staff in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he says, under number 3: "As the prison in Vogosca is considered illegal by our legal regulations, this prison is to be immediately transformed into a department of penitentiary and correctional facility in Butmir or Pale and investigative judge as well as warden to be appointed. This is the task the Ministry of Justice." What was illegal about the prison there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The item 3 of this letter seems to be written by a layperson. Who could bring an investigating judge? Of course, the Ministry of Justice is in charge. There were two prisons there, formed by -- set up by the Vogosca municipality. But with the establishment of the Ministry of Justice and with the establishment of prisons, remand prisons attached to district courts, this prison was abolished. And the prisoners were transferred to military prisons, if they were military personnel, and civilians were released; whereas, persons under investigation were transferred to courts. All these local prisons were abolished, prisons that were set up in all sorts of gymnasiums and similar buildings. The man rightly said they were illegal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So this -- was this an example of the problem that you had been discussing at government level about prisons and -- and treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you say "civilians were released," do you mean people who didn't come under the category of either those had who had committed crimes or those who had carried arms?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was within the purview of the state commission which cooperated with the commission of the Federation. They checked between themselves the status of prisoners and the exchange of prisoners and the release of civilians and other persons. It was not only the ministry who decided who was a civilian or not; it was the state commission for exchange and the army, which had sole responsibility under military provisions to release non-Serbs detained in various prisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. Can we just look at that answer for a moment. You say that it was the army that had sole responsibility under military provisions to release non-Serbs detained in various persons. If the army had arrested combatants or whatever and declared them prisoners of war and placed them in places like Manjaca, then presumably they had responsibility for the prisoners. But what happened if police had arrested people and put them in prison?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that belonged to the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor's office, they were transferred to the military prosecutor's office. If something fell within the jurisdiction of civilian prosecution, they were transferred to civilian Prosecution. However, in actual fact, 5 per cent -- sorry, 95 per cent fell within the jurisdiction of the military prosecution because they abandoned the front lines, deserted, and -- for various other reasons. That's why I asked that at certain point in time to integrate all that and to introduce the rule of law. Because the civilian prosecution, once established, had little to do. And the military prosecution, which had a lot of work to do, had not been established. And lots of problems were perpetuated by that in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness is, again, talking very fast, and I believe at least 30 per cent was not recorded with -- what he said. Then what is recorded appears not to -- to have much sense in my opinion. So maybe we can ask the witness to repeat his answer from the beginning slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, provided it's knocked off my time, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'm afraid, as you've heard from Mr. Zecevic, you're speaking quite fast. And it's important that we get the full translation of your answer. You were talking about or I asked you about if civilian police arrested someone and placed them in prison who would have the authority to deal with them, and you then gave an answer in respect of -- as I understand it, you said that if something fell within the civilian prosecution, they were transferred to civilian prosecution. And then you went on to say that 95 per cent fell within the jurisdiction of the military prosecution. Now, can you just explain what you were talking about, quite slowly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If something happened involving damage to property or injury to a person or God forbid a killing or something and the civilian police comes out, during the on-site investigation they establish exactly what it's about, whether the crime concerned belongs to military prosecution or civilian prosecution. All persons between 18 to 55 years of age fell under the jurisdiction of the military prosecution and military judiciary. So 95 per cent of all offences fell within the jurisdiction of the military prosecution and judiciary. The civilian police would come to a crime scene, establish that it concerns the military prosecution, and submit it to military prosecution. However, if they establish it falls under the jurisdiction of the civilian prosecution, they hand the case over to civilian prosecution. But that happened very seldom. Although, in my opinion, the civilian prosecution was better organised at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what I really want to deal with was you've told us that the definition of a civilian would be a matter for whoever was in charge of -- of the prisons. What did -- what was your definition is what I want to know, Mr. Mandic, of what a civilian was who was released? Because you said civilians were released.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only authority that could decide who was a civilian or not was the army, the commander of that territory. And that was under the decree of the minister in charge of the army and on the orders of the president of the Republic. Namely, that the status of detainees had to be established beyond doubt. So nobody but the commander of the army on that territory was competent. It was clearly stipulated in the -- in the decree, in the military decree, written by Bogdan Subotic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's -- leaving aside areas where there were military manoeuvres going on or military action, in an area where, for example, there was no fighting going on at all, who would decide who had been wrongly placed in -- in prison, who was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the competent military commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Even though people who had been, let's say, picked up and placed in prison in Vogosca who were civilians, because you've just told us civilians were released?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Major Trifunovic was in charge for the territory of Vogosca and he was the only one authorised to say who was a civilian or not. Not a civilian authority, not the police force could do that, because the state of immediate threat of war had been declared already, and everything was the responsibility of the military commander in the given area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So as far as you were concerned, this Mr. Poplasen who was saying that there was an illegal prison and being kept there and that civilians - as you told us, although the document doesn't say that - should be released, that was decided entirely by the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the army could do that in cooperation with the Crisis Staff of the given municipality. However, the last word belonged to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move, then, shall we, please, to the transcript of the 17th Session of the Assembly. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 928, please. Which was held in July of -- oh, sorry, no, I think it's been exhibited. P199.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, tab 71.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, I take it you were there. This was in July, 24th to 26th of July. And in a large part it dealt with the setting up of the organisation of courts and judges and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at page 6 in English; and in B/C/S, it's the fifth page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, well it must -- it's not the fifth page in B/C/S then. Well, it should be. But we should have -- yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see that item 20 is: "Decision regarding the organisation and jurisdictions of military courts and military prosecutors." Decision on the actual jurisdiction of regular courts, basic courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go, please, to page 7 in English and page 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see there item 47 -- well, item 42 and 41 -- sorry. Decision founding a state documentation centre for researching of war crimes against Serbs? Decision 42: Appointing the director of state documentation centre for researching of war crimes against Serbs. And then 47: Foca, basic court, Trebinje, Visegrad, and so on and so forth. And then if we go down the page we see prosecutors. Is that right? So that was the first major Assembly, or that was the first Assembly that dealt in a large part with the judicial system?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could you confirm you were actually present?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably was, since the agenda included so many affairs in the purview of the justice ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just ask you to consider something that was said by, I believe it was Mr. Krajisnik in his introduction. No. I believe it was Mr. Micic. Oh, no. I'm so sorry, it was Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, it's at page 18 of the document in English; and it's at page 15 in the Cyrillic. And it's about halfway down -- it's at the top -- I believe it's the top of the page in the Cyrillic and it's halfway down in English. It's a sentence beginning: "Militarily ..." It's about halfway through the page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, they can't hear you, Mr. Mandic. Have you found the paragraph that begins: "Militarily we are in an excellent position"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking, for the purposes of the English, please, if we could highlight from approximately halfway down the page. That's it. Absolutely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Militarily we are in an excellent position; our foreign political position is terrible; our domestic political situation is very good, being that our people are fully in favour of fighting, that is, peace. Because we do not have any more reason to fight, we have liberated almost everything that is ours. In final talks we could even return some territories and villages that do not belong to us." Now, did you understand that what was being said was that everything that the Serbs had claimed was their territory had, in fact, almost been achieved and, indeed, some things had been taken which didn't belong to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only comment. I was not really knowledgeable about those military tasks and conquests. I really don't know. I don't have an opinion. Is that Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's Mr. Krajisnik. Well -- I mean, you were a minister in the government and you were attending government meetings. Was there any discussion about the fact that in the course of this military action in fact territories had been seised and villages that actually couldn't even remotely be claimed as Serb?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Government is the civilian authority of state administration. For military affairs, there was another body in charge consisting of five or six people in the top military echelon and the government never discussed military successes or actions or failures. Look at all the minutes; you will see that they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how I read the page 8 in Serbian, those are the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... well, in that case, can I ask the witness to read it out and we'll get a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because the different person is talking; it's not Mr. Karadzic. That's what I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I didn't say it was Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I say it was -- it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, you say it was Karadzic, do you? All right, sorry. I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't mean there is something wrong with the translation here, you mean that the speaker is mis -- I have misidentified the speaker?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because you said that Mr. Krajisnik is talking. And it's apparent that Mr. Krajisnik gives the floor to the president of Republika Srpska. So those are the words of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm perfectly prepared to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the -- Mr. Karadzic, as we've heard, and -- I mean, it was the supreme commander of the army, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you telling us that you -- there was never any discussion about the fact that in the course of -- of carrying out the objectives of the -- of the government of the Republika Srpska, the army had gone further?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the fighting, the combat, there was a military command headed by the President of the Republic. And there were people who did that only and discussed only about that. I believe there were members of the Presidency in that circle, the President, Biljana Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic, Mr. Karadzic, Branko Djeric, and probably the minister of defence or not I'm sure, and Ratko Mladic. These people discussed these affairs and informed the MPs about losses and gains in territory. We, in the government, did not discuss these things. We are the civilian authority concentrating on completely different things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I just want to ask you one other -- two other things, maybe, about this meeting in the five minutes before the break. Can you go -- could we go in English, please, to page 65 and in the B/C/S to page 67, where the gentleman who you had the phone conversation, Mr. Prstojevic, speaks. And what he says here is: "When the Serbs started the uprising in Sarajevo and when they seised control over certain territories, there was no government or at least it was not known where it was then. Didn't even know Mr. Karadzic was alive. When we learnt he was alive and when he visited us in Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of territories where they'd actually been in a majority." Now, that appears to be carrying along the same line from what Mr. Karadzic was saying. You knew Mr. Prstojevic, and you rang him up to tell him to stop driving Muslims out. Had he actually taken any notice of what you'd said to him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learned about those activities of his from Tomo Kovac a few days before. And in one intercept I even suggested to Kovac that he arrest or kill the man because he was creating problems to everyone in Ilidza, the authorities and the police. He was really destructive. And, you see, he was denying the existence of the government and that Radovan Karadzic was alive, et cetera. My opinion of Mr. Prstojevic and his ilk could not be worse. Those people created most of the problems, and many of them ended up here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you see -- but, Mr. Mandic, to your knowledge, did anybody stand up in the Assembly that you were at and say what Mr. Prstojevic just said is - or words to that effect - is an outrage, and what he has done is illegal and a crime?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Prstojevic was a member of the parliament or in what capacity he was speaking. I wasn't really listening. That man didn't interest me. I didn't want to know his views or listen to his speeches. They obstructed the government and everything that was going on. He wasn't even an extremist. I think it was all grand standing and attempts to ingratiate themselves to the Serbian leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, in fact, at the end of that session - and I don't think I need to trouble you - all the decisions were taken in respect of the courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is this a convenient point to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It would be, Your Honour, yes, because it's the end of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the -- while the witness is ushered in, I have an intervention in the transcript, 31, line 4, first, I suggested -- I believe the witness said, I suggested to Tomo Kovac to arrest him, meaning, Prstojevic, because he was creating problems to everyone in Ilidza. And then 31, 9, he said, Those people created most of the problems, and because of them many others ended up here in The Hague. That is what the witness says. Maybe this can be clarified with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not at all sure what -- what Mr. Zecevic wants clarified. Perhaps Mr. Zecevic can just repeat what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, page 31, line 4, the witness, I believe, said - and this can be clarified: I suggested to Tomo Kovac that he should arrest Prstojevic because he was creating problems to everyone in Ilidza. That's one thing. And the second thing is page 31, line 9, it is recorded as: "Those people created most of the problems, and many of them ended up here in The Hague." That is not what he said. He says: "Because of them, many others ended up in The Hague." That is -- that was the intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, did you hear that? I certainly agree that I heard you say that you suggested that Kovac arrest Mr. Prstojevic. And do you agree that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have this intercept in your documents where I state that Kovac should arrest Prstojevic. And I said that because of him and people like him, many other peoples ended up in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people like Prstojevic, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Mandic, can I ask you briefly to look at another intercept. I'm afraid that we skipped forward to July by mistake, because I would like to stay in June for a bit. Could you have a look, please, at the document which is numbered P1134 this -- oh, sorry, it's tab 73. Sorry, Mr. Zecevic. It's a conversation between you and Mr. Krajisnik on the 26th of June, and I think maybe we'd better just look at the context. At the bottom of page 1 in English Mr. Krajisnik asks you how does -- how is everything go. And then over to page 2 in English and -- and in B/C/S. And Krajisnik then says that -- there are two things: He wanted to see if Stanisic was there, to see what is happening with this. And it's not at all clear. I don't know whether you can assist, Mr. Mandic. It would probably help if I give you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or if Mr. Zecevic, perhaps, would be kind enough to give the -- because mine's marked, would it be possible to give over your -- the B/C/S copy? That would be -- I think it's easier for Mr. Mandic if he just looks at it. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... was reading. I wasn't following what you were asking, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you just have a look, please, very quickly, Mr. Mandic, at the first page and at the context. It's not clear what that's about. And then on to the second page where he -- Mr. Krajisnik says: "I wanted to see if Stanisic was there, to see with him what is happening with this."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, in fact, what I wanted to ask but was this. Krajisnik asks you at the bottom of the third page: "Have you released the one I told you about by any chance?" And you said: "Yes." And he repeated yes. And then you said: "He left for Vrbanja approximately one hour ago." And Krajisnik said: "Thank God." And you said: "Karamehmedovic, right?" And that he's gone. Now, can you tell us what -- clearly you released somebody called the name I have so much difficulty with, Karamehmedovic; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's probably a friend of President Momcilo Krajisnik. He was probably somewhere in the Serb territory, and I took him to Vrbanja, which was on the border between the Serb and Muslim-held territories. Probably he left for Sarajevo via Vrbanja. This is probably what this is all about. But I can't recall this conversation. But this is definitely to do with a person of Muslim ethnicity as far as I can discern from this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, it says "released." So do we take it from that that this gentleman was, in fact, a prisoner somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But, did you -- all I want to know, actually, was did you have the authority, as the minister of justice, to order the release of people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't have that kind of authority. Only the army could do that, if non-Serbs were detained. Now, whether I went to see some of the commanders and asked him to release this person or whether it was on Krajisnik's intervention, I can't say. This is the first time I'm seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you see, because -- he's saying not: "Have you arranged with the army to release it," but he is saying to you: "Have you released the one ..." Which is why I'm asking you the question. Isn't it right that you did actually have the authority to get people released, non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have that authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to the next part which is the part that I'm also interested in. Mr. Krajisnik says: "What about Milos Savic? And you said: "President, I put it on the list. The first exchange it will be finished. Check it down there, do have you anyone down there, can you contact someone?" And you say: "There is this Vukic, a member of the youth organisation, a Serb, who is criticising because we have 400 prisoners here, you know." And Mr. Krajisnik said: "Who is criticising?" And you said: "I've got 400. "And who is criticising?" Repeats Mr. Krajisnik. That this Filip Vukovic, the member of the youth organisation. Now, were those 400 anything to do with the list of 400 that we saw a way back in May, the list of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that the state commission compiled lists and carried out exchanges. This Vukovic was probably the chairman of the commission from the Federation for exchange of POWs. These exchanges took place in Lukavica in the penal/correctional facility Butmir. And the state commission for exchange could not carry out exchanges without such lists. This was the government commission that was established I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but -- I'm sorry, the -- Mr. Vukovic is apparently a member of a youth organisation, nothing to do with -- with the -- well, he's the -- sorry, I beg your pardon. He's the president of the exchange commission. But you're saying "We have 400 prisoners." Now what I'm asking is: Are those 400 anything to do with the list of 400 that we saw from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovic was the chairman of the exchange commission on behalf of the Federation. He was a youth executive before the war in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm saying here that there were 400 people in Lukavica to be exchanged by the state commission, and he was the chairman of that commission. He was well known as Tito's youth, who he was the president of the youth organisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were those 400 people, were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know, Madam Prosecutor. I don't know who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll leave that. Thank you very much. I don't want to spend any more time on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go next, please, to a document which is P1157. Tab 76.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a conversation between you and Mr. Karadzic on the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go, please, to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he's asking you - Mr. Karadzic - first of all, What's up, Momo?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not on the right page, just a moment, in the B/C/S. Yes. And -- that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say: "Not much. I have just been to a government session, and I'm here." And you say: "We're working on an exchange now. We're evacuating some Serbs from Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija?" "Very important," says Karadzic. "We'll immediately mobilise those fit for combat. How many will there be? "I don't really know. We have many on the list." And then you say: "There are 300 people from Hadzici, Muslims who have been kept here for seven days. No one's inquired about them. No one seems to care. I don't know what to do." You say: "Nobody's interested in them." And finally you say: "... so we'll try to exchange them for people from Hrasnica." Now, these 300 people from Hadzici, where were they being kept?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as can I remember, at the time, the Chairman of the exchange commission resigned. And I personally coordinated the work of the state commission for exchange when the exchanges were being carried out in Butmir between the two warring parties. They were kept at the penal and correctional facility in Butmir, and they had been brought in from the culture centre in Hadzici when all these local centres were being closed all across Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So they were being kept in Butmir, or Kula I think it was called --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were kept in a gym in Hadzici, if I remember correctly. And they were brought to Butmir to be exchanged. A list was made, and the exchange was to take place at the airfield which was 100 metres from the penal and correctional facility building. And I informed the president of the Republic, among other people, about this. However, this commission that was led by Filip Vukovic from the Federation didn't want to take these people on board because they didn't have space to provide accommodation for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say that nobody inquired about them, nobody seems to care. What sort of people were they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. They were probably civilians, because only exchange was involved. People were to be released, but the other side didn't want to receive them because they didn't have enough space to accommodate them in Sarajevo. I really can't remember what their actual status was. I coordinated the work of all these state commissions for exchange of POWs. And I was down there on a completely different errand, because President Karadzic had asked me to locate a Croat and to let him go to Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going come on to that because we see that's the next part of the conversation. So it's not just Mr. Krajisnik who wants you to release people. Mr. Karadzic was also asking you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He had sent me to find this man and to do my best to release him and let him go to Split. That was a completely private matter for President Karadzic. This person was a friend of his. He had lived in Sarajevo, and he had many friend there is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But this is the point, Mr. Mandic, that we keep coming back to. You keep saying only the army could order release. But this is clearly a man who is in prison at Kula who is a friend of Mr. Karadzic. He is asking to you release him, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. Look at the beginning of the conversation. I first talk to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sipcic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he was the one who decided who would be released or not, as a corps commander. And he was the only one who could either approve or disprove of someone's release. No one could be either detained or released without his knowledge. Now, the fact that I intervened and asked for this favour, of course, a corps commander would try to do his best and to fulfil the request of the President. I was just a mediator in the whole affair.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, I'm sorry, nowhere in this conversation is there any suggestion that he is the one who is going to arrange the release. Is there, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was I who organised it and arranged it, but he had given approval. Of course, a corps commander was not going to go and look for some person. It was up to me to conduct this private arrangement for this Croat to be released because I spent most of the time down there. I wasn't either in Sarajevo or at Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, the conversation about this family, in fact, because it talks about three brothers, goes on. And you say you will make further inquires and call him back in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's on the third page in English and also in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then further down I just want to ask you about this, please. Mr. Karadzic says: "The thing with the Greeks should be strengthened." And you say: "I don't know." And then you say: "Our Mico has left, hasn't he?" Who are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know which Mico I was referring to. There were at least ten of them, Mico Majicic [as interpreted], Mico Stanisic, Mico Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, maybe the context will help you, because Karadzic says: "I don't know why he's doing this after all." And you say: "I don't. "He's not suitable for this kind of thing at all." And you said: "I don't get this thing, Mr. President. I mean, if we need to have someone up there to coordinate things, we can, but we need someone to work permanently on the establishment of such a service." Now, does that help you as to which Mico you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Could it be someone from the State Security Service? Mico Polic? I don't know. Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's not guess. All right, thank you. That's all I want to ask you about this. Now can we go back, please, to the question of the appointments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look at document number 2722, which is tab 77.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a document dated the 6th of July, and it's actually -- it appears from the public prosecutor's office in Banja Luka. And it says: "Please find attached a list of" -- somebody carefully stamped draft translation over it, but I think it says, "deputies to the," something, prosecution, "prosecutor who are being nominated with brief personal information ..." Now is this a document that you got?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This document was addressed and sent to Banja Luka municipality for coordination, pursuant to an initiative by the prosecutor proposing his deputy. Once it has been coordinated in Banja Luka, then it would have been sent to the ministry in Sarajevo. This was an internal regional coordination of personnel to fill the positions of deputy prosecutors. The public prosecutor made his proposals to Banja Luka municipalities -- for his deputies. That was according to the law, and once it has been agreed, then this kind of harmonised and dovetailed document would then be sent to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. As we'll see from the discussion at the Assembly, you obviously did at some stage get this document. But can we just look very quickly at some of the nationalities of those who were proposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, first of all, the first two pages for persons nominated all deal with Serbs, because the ethnicity or nationality is given. Could we go to the fourth page of this document. Sorry, it's the third page in B/C/S. Third page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 11, Ahmed Kapetanovic, who is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six, 7, and 5 are also Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm sorry, but we lost the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So did we.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at numbers 6 and 7, their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Mr. Mandic, I'm afraid there's a technical problem at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand it will be corrected in about five minutes. Is counsel terribly handicapped by the loss of the LiveNote? Do we have to take a break, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's working on this. It's only not working on -- yes, if we could go on. It's not working on ours, but it's working here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can. As far as the Defence is concerned, we can proceed, because we have it on the -- on the central monitor. We don't have on our monitors. But if it's a sort time, we can live with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mandic, you were saying -- All right, let's go back -- can we go back, please -- you say 5, 6, and 7 were non-Serbs. I don't think so. Not for prosecutors. Can we go back, please, to the second -- I'm sorry, it's the third page in English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Look at the list of judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry. I'm coming to judges. Was the prosecutors, one prosecutor, number 11, was -- Now let's look at the judges --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, fifth page in English and fourth page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 3 of the proposed judges is a Croat. Number 5 is a Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go, please, in English to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... coming. The English doesn't correspond with the same page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's number 9, not number 8, is a Muslim. Mirsada Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we go, please, in English to page 7, and in B/C/S, to - one, two, three, four, five - fifth page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 13, a Croat. Number 14, a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 19, although it's crossed out, Mr. Pejic was a Yugoslav. He declared himself a Yugoslav. But by his name, what nationality would he be it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be a Serb, it could be a Croat. The Pejic surname is common to both.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 20 also declared herself a Yugoslav. From the name, a Muslim, [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a Muslim first name and a Muslim last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then number 24 -- could, we go -- we need to see the next page, because that says --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slovenka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's a Slovenian. Number 25, Muslim; number 26, Muslim; number 29, although it's crossed out, a Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then we need to go to the next page in English, please. Number 35. And the next page in B/C/S. Number 35 is a Croat. And to number 4 -- the rest, I believe, on that page, the next are all Serbs. Number 44, which is on the next page and in B/C/S as well. Number 44 is a Muslim. And I think that's it. And then, finally, could we look at the note which is on the next page in English, and -- yeah. No, sorry, oh, yes, no, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And item number C: "In accordance with the agreement reached with the members of the Ministry of Justice" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we need to go over the page English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... we have respected ethnic parity." And it's signed by Mr. Radic, dated the 13th of July. Now, did you, at some stage, even if not in this form, get the list of candidates like this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did receive nominations and then we made appointments or, rather, we submitted nomination to the president of the republic to sign appointments for various municipalities. And it is certain that in Banja Luka people of all ethnicities were enrolled in both the prosecutor's office and in the judiciary, people who fulfilled all the requires for the posts. Because in our letters, we would ask the principle of ethnic parity to be respected, equal representation of various ethnic groups, as per the ethnic structure at the moment of the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask that this be admitted and marked, because you will see that it is connected with the next document that I'm going to show. I know he didn't get it in this particular form, but he says he is aware of the nominations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1326, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I now want to you have a look, please, at the Assembly session at which you were certainly present because you spoke where these appointments were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is, please, document number 7 -- P738, tab 93.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was actually held on the 12th of August in Banja Luka.
