And after Mr. Krajisnik opened the session, you spoke, you see, and said you propose to include in the agenda the election and the appointment of the judges of the Banja Luka lower court and deputy prosecutor in Banja Luka. So you were clearly there, Mr. Mandic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move to the taking of the vote, which we will see on page 24, I hope, in English. And in the B/C/S -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's quite [indiscernible]. Sorry, it's not that far. I made a mistake. Sorry, Your Honours. I'll just ... Yes. Sorry, yes I've got it. It's page -- first of all, 10 in English; and then in B/C/S, it's the same page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see there that the first item in the agenda is the appointment of judges. And you speak again about 50 judges being proposed. And Mr. Krajisnik - is this right, because it just says chairman, I think - says, I hereby open a separate debate on every judge, separately. And the first one is Vesna Antonic. Now, this is why I asked you about Bijeljina because what he says is this: "I would only like to reiterate the conclusions from a session in Pale when we discussed the appointment of judges to the lower court in Bijeljina. At that time Mr. Bijelic gave an acceptable explanation that we should not appoint judges of different nationality until the issue is resolved, that this will be a state of Serbs and other citizens while the rights of citizens and positions to which they can be appointed would be decided later. Therefore, I believe, if we reach such conclusions in Pale, we could then delay the appointment of judges until a constitution precisely defines which position citizens of other nationalities can occupy. Perhaps, even here, we should proceed in this manner and appoint only the proposed Serb judges, while the Croat and Muslim candidates would be appointed only if the constitution which we are definitely going to change ensures such rights for them." And then Mr. Bijelic spoke?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we go over the page in the English, please, to the next speaker. Mr. Brdjanin. I need the next page, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He says about halfway -- well, Therefore let's not take this off the agenda but remove five or six of the proposed people. I am submitting yesterday's proposal for revision to the high court in Banja Luka because neither Mr. Kupresanin or Mr. Vukic are behind these proposals; I talked to them this morning. Therefore, let us appoint only those judges who are of Serbian nationality. We cannot say this to Europe or the rest of the world, but we can say it here between ourselves. Now, you heard that, Mr. Mandic. What view did you take of what Mr. Brdjanin was saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained it a moment ago. I can try again. There were certainly some MPs, including Milojevic, Prstojevic, and Brdjanin, who wanted a mono-ethnic state and mono-ethnic selection of prosecutors and judges and other staff in the judiciary. I did not agree with it, and Dr. Karadzic did not agree with it. And despite everything, we elected into the municipal prosecutor's office and the municipal court judges of all ethnic communities, despite the views of these MPs who put forward their personal opinions. And that was true in other municipalities too. And at least while I was minister --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I managed to ensure that proportionate representation is observed in the prosecutor's offices and the judiciary. But, of course, there were opposing views as well, but all these people were subsequently eventually appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's have a look, please, at these appointments, shall we? If we go -- Mr. Popovic supports the no Serbs to be appointed. If we then look at the chairman, he goes through the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at the next page in English and the -- page 13 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Appointed is Vesna Radeta-Antonic, a Serb. Mr. Babic -- if we go over the page in English. Ruza Blagojevic, a Croat, who is in favour -- no, not appointed. Ms. Bursac, a Serb. And then a Montenegrin, Mr. Cvijanovic. And then we come down to number 8, Dusanka Fazlic, a Serb, daughter of Avdo - which causes some hilarity, apparently - not appointed. On the basis, Mr. Mandic, is this right, that from her name she wasn't a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with it. People can decide what ethnic group they belong to, regardless of their name. But I can tell you that all these people were eventually appointed, although they didn't pass at this Assembly meeting, at my insistence and the insistence of Mr. Karadzic, and they ended up occupying those posts. At this time, the nationalist fraction got the upper hand, and these people were not approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's the point. To save me a long and rather tedious exercise, Mr. Mandic, not one single candidate for this position who was not a Serb or a Montenegrin was elected in this Assembly, were they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. At this Assembly meeting. But later, they were elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Ms. Korner, page 16, in all fairness to the witness, page 16, under number 13 and number 14, both are Croats and have been appointed on this Assembly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I -- you're absolutely right, and I'm open to correction if there's anybody else. I missed those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the next page, 25, the Muslim woman, 26, Muslim woman, one Yugoslav, one Italian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... sorry just a moment. Yes. Sorry, number -- sorry, 25, a Muslim, not elected. 26, a Muslim, not collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's why I say I'm open to -- I agree -- it's a long and tedious exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I raise the issue with number 13 and number 14 who have been -- number 13 has been elected. He's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that. So out of -- I take that entirely. And, as I say, I'm open to correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So out of that long list that we saw and we went through, one Croat, Zoran Lipovac, a Croat, was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move, then, please, to the -- just one thing, yes. Can we look at page 23 in English, and -- and in B/C/S, to page 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Somebody called Slobodanka Hrvacanin. Do you know who she was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think she was an MP in the Assembly of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She is taking here objection to, in fact, a Serb, Mr. Krkeljas who -- see says: This Serb has more inflicted more evil on us Zenica Serbs than any Muslim who lives there. Although I'm an Orthodox Serb, as Brdjanin said, I'd rather vote for every single Muslim for Mr. Krkeljas. He's openly distanced himself from Serbs and SDS of which he was never a member. He's argued with us in the newspapers and caused us immense evil. So she took objection to that on the basis that he was a Serb who wasn't supporting the SDS. Now can we look, please, at the prosecutors which is on the next page. Deputy prosecutors, I'm afraid. And there we see Mr. Kapetanovic, the gentleman who was at the end of the list that we looked at earlier, who is in favour, none, I declare, he's not been appointed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's number 11, sorry. You need to go to the next page in B/C/S; I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the judges of the higher court, which is on the next page in English but the same page in B/C/S. Mr. Bajagic, a Montenegrin, doesn't pass. Mr. Dukic, a Croat, does not pass. And then we come to Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: High court judges, please, at page 27 in English and page 27 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only one who causes discussion is Mr. Vukotic, a Montenegrin, and he doesn't pass. All right. Now, Mr. Mandic, you were there at this Assembly, and as you've said it was clear that the deputies weren't going to elect, were they, non-Serbs to these positions, one, with the exception that has been pointed out by Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you have seen, the Ministry of Justice issued instructions as to how to appoint officials of the prosecution and the judiciary, and this Mr. Radic in Banja Luka honoured this, that the MPs didn't. I cannot comment on the decisions of the parliament and the MPs. Of course, they were not right. But I have expressed my view through these documents how people should be chosen into the judiciary and the prosecutor's office, but the parliament is the highest authority in the state. But I'm telling you again these people were eventually appointed with the approval of Mr. Karadzic and at my insistence. They worked as long as they worked. I don't know if they remained in Banja Luka until the end of the war, because I left very soon afterwards. And, of course, there were people among the MPs who believed that only Serbs should occupy positions in the Serb state. It's a well-known fact, people like this, Prstojevic, Brdjanin, I don't know who else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just then move on, please, to ask you about something that Mr. Grahovac said, which is page 52 in English and it is ... page 50 in B/C/S, to begin with, anyhow, the part I want. Mr. Grahovac, did you know him? He was obviously -- he was a deputy, but did you know him as someone who came from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. He talks about Mr. Brdjanin, and then he talks about the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at the next page in English and the next page in B/C/S. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, he is in the middle of a rant about Mr. Brdjanin, saying that he spreads his own people in leading positions, his own cadres, in that way he would have absolute power. And then he says: "I understand this is perhaps a concession regarding the quashing of this autonomism and so on. If that's the solution, then there is no problem, since I'm always ready to prevent certain concrete information on what had happened in our MUP. I don't want to say that Mr. Brdjanin actively took part in that, but it is certain that did he cover things up to some extent, those dirty dealings with our chief Stojan Zupljanin. I said that I will say these things at the Assembly session since it is my Assembly. I am a deputy in it. I know that the department of Mr. Zupljanin stolen [sic] cars from Banja were registered." And he talks about the Suzuki and so on. Former cadres took part in that. Communists, among which is Stojan Zupljanin, they accused me of certain abuses and similar things. Now, were you aware of what he was referring to, as an ex-minister of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never a minister of the interior. I don't know. I don't know how you expect me to comment on the statements and contributions by individual members of the Assembly and what this was all about. This was 18 years ago. Now, these squabbles between MPs from Krajina, I was not au courant and I cannot comment. I really have no idea. I don't even know who this man is, what's his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mandic, I don't want to go through it because you were asked about it, but you knew about and got involved in the whole sorry saga of the business of the Volkswagen Golfs from TAS, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm not suggesting -- there was -- I don't want to go through it because it is not the purpose, Mr. Mandic, but there was a massive argument, wasn't there, in 1995 -- at the 50th Assembly about the Golfs, and indeed you were there, and about some article, some interview had you given to a Belgrade magazine about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, believe me, what the press was writing. As far for the Volkswagen Golfs, I believe the Assembly received a report about that, and the minister, Mico Stanisic, informed the Assembly in detail, the report was accepted, and I personal had nothing to do with any vehicles or Golfs or whatever. I was minister of justice until 1992 and then I left to live in Belgrade. Now, what the press was writing about, this political turmoil and the political squabbles among politicians, I know nothing about that and I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, as I say, I don't want to spend too much time on this. Allegations were made and cross-allegations that you and other politicians had benefitted, wasn't it, from this -- the thefts and -- from the Golfs, of the Golfs from the factory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, not a single Golf was stolen from Pretis Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think that's all that I need ask you about ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can I just ask you -- I'm sorry, there's one other thing I want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, at page 74. And then you again. And it's page 71 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the vice-president of the Assembly, Branko Simic. He was originally from Mostar in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He says --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, of course, he was an MP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "I am of the opinion that today's session of the Serbian Assembly was abused and used for giving lectures to Serbian deputies. I responsibly claim from this stand you do not know Serbian soldiers, that you only assume. If five Muslim judges in Banja Luka would prevent a foreign intervention, dear colleagues, Serbian deputies, I propose, then, we leave the Serbian justice system to the Muslims. Another thing, dear friend, you do not have the bad experience which I and my colleagues have had. They slaughtered our children, raped our sisters, raped young Serbian girls. To have a preliminary judge try a Serbian soldier in war time, that is impossible. They will turn the Serbian People and the Serbian soldiers against us. Now, Mr. Mandic, you heard that because we'll see you spoke a moment later. In your view, if he was the Deputy Speaker, or whatever, of the Assembly - I seem to have lost the LiveNote - was this a proper speech to be making?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not up to me to assess the speeches delivered by individual MPs and to interfere in the Assembly debates. Everybody in that war had their own personal wounds and traumas, people lost their families. It was inappropriate for me to speak against such people. If somebody had lost a child or had somebody killed in the war, and it was not up to me to say a Muslim cannot be a judge in such proceedings. That wouldn't be appropriate. That would have been very ugly. I was of the opinion that people who were professional and expert in their job, regardless of their nationality, should remain there. You can see that from the Official Gazette, and you can see there the composition of the courts and the prosecutor's offices, et cetera. Wherever it was possible for me to push through my intentions and my ideas, I did that. However, if the Assembly failed to vote in favour of my proposal and the proposal of the municipality involved, then it was up to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all right. That's all I want to ask you about the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move very quickly, please, to document 1395 at tab 78, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a ruling from the Vogosca municipal secretariat, apparently, adopting that the house of Almas Planja and Miralem Planja is being allocated for use to the Ministry of Justice for the needs of the prison department of Vogosca Serb municipality, temporary character. And this is pursuant to a request by the Ministry of Justice, Butmir Prison Department of The Vogosca Serb municipality? Was this something that you were aware of, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the area of Vogosca, Ilijas and Hadzici municipalities, the court number 2 was set up. And for the needs of that court, we wanted to have investigation or, rather, detention premises to serve the court. The municipality of Vogosca gave us two or three rooms in the military prison that had been there since the beginning of the war. When the international community forces took over the airport, the Serbian territory was cut off. And to reach these municipalities, one has to take an 80-kilometre roundabout way. We had to make sure that courts functioned in that area and for that purpose we set up one court for these three municipalities and we asked for detention or prison premises to be provided for that court, and I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This was clearly, wasn't it, a house that belonged to some Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a man who was living in Germany at the time, and his house was converted into a military prison in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever get any complaints about the treatment of people who were being kept there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the jurisdiction of the Municipal Court II, which was in charge of individual cases, I've never heard any such complaints. Actually, during my term of office, I think that only one or two people were remanded in that prison during investigation. It was a woman and a young man. And that was done within the jurisdiction of the judges of regular courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1327, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, now at document 1987. This is a document -- is that signed by you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So somebody signed -- I think it says -- does it say "za" and then a signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then it's dated 5th of August and it says that you sent a letter, well, Ministry of Justice, I should say, to the Presidency proposing that the regular courts and public prosecutor's offices temporarily take over the competence of military courts et cetera. And you -- the Presidency hasn't informed the ministry about it's opinion as regards this proposal. So that's what you have been referring to all along, that you made this proposal, that the civilian and military courts be, as it were, joined for a period?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1328, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you look, please, at a document that has already been exhibited but I want to ask you about it, P191. This is a document from Dr. Karadzic which is addressed to -- well, it says: "The Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Justice are given the task of obtaining, via municipal organs of the interior and administrations of houses of correction on the territory of the Serbian republic ... official written reports on the treatment and behaviour by Serbian authorities of prisoners of war and the living conditions ... held in prisons in municipalities where such cases exist." Was it the television report on Omarska and places that had prompted this, Mr. Mandic; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we, then, look, please, at document 2650, tab 86.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is Mr. Poplasen again. And it's addressed to the Ministry of Justice, asking for approval for occasional use of detainees for construction and other work according to the current needs. And: "We ask for an urgent follow-up of this conclusion." Did you get this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And this was not signed by Nikola Poplasen. The Ministry of Justice was not competent to send someone to perform work. It was solely the military commander, pursuant to minister's order, to assign someone to carry out works. So this was an erroneously addressed letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you see, I mean, I know you keep saying this, Mr. Mandic, but the Vogosca prison was a prison under civilian authority, not military, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. It -- it was a military prison in Vogosca, which was run by Brano Vlaco, appointed by the military authorities; and the commander of Vogosca Brigade, Trifunovic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But we've just seen a document you accept you did get where the Planja's House is to be turned into a part of the Vogosca prison system. So it wasn't all military, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of it was under the jurisdiction of the Municipal Court II, headquartered in Vogosca but only for the needs and purposes of that court. So one section of the prison. Just like in Scheveningen, you have you one section which is for The Hague Tribunal and the other section is used by the Dutch judiciary. It was just a building that was divided into two sections, but there was no intertwining of jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, leaving aside whether this was actually signed by Mr. Poplasen. It was obviously signed on his behalf; as we can see, "za." If there was no jurisdiction to grant permission for prisoners to work, why was this letter being addressed to the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of ignorance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It has been corrected because your question was a part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Mr. Poplasen you knew, and he had been certainly working on prisons and the like for months. How could he -- you perhaps can't answer that, but is there anything about Mr. Poplasen that led you to believe he was ignorant enough to ask permission from the Ministry of Justice for permission that they could not grant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, Nikola Poplasen was not working at prison. He was a commissioner of the Presidency for Vogosca municipality. I can't believe that he didn't know that it was only up to the army to -- to determine whether non-Serbs would go to perform construction and other works. That was a well-known ordinary, and every commander in every municipality and every prison had this order and were aware of it. There are documents supporting that. There are documents indicating that nobody else except the military commander was authorised to send non-Serbs to perform labour. This was an order published in the Official Gazette 6/92, signed by Bogdan Subotic, pursuant to the authorisation of President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, is this a convenient point?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I don't know -- Mr. Mandic says he never received this document. It -- it's there for all to see. I obviously would like to have it exhibited. But if you feel that I have not laid sufficient groundwork, then I would ask for it to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, on the subject, Your Honours, very briefly. We object to this because the witness said that this is not the signature of Nikola Poplasen, so I -- I believe in this case, again, we have the situation where the -- the document does not reach the threshold to be even MFI'd. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but it clear says "za" on this document. Your Honours, as I say --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, I mean, it's -- I don't think there is another witness that we can deal with it. But if Your Honours feel that it will have to be dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll marked it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1329, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought Your Honour said you want to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so we will take the break at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at document 1324, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a decision by Dr. Karadzic dated 6th of August, 1992, that says that the Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Justice are obliged to obtain official written information in a coordinated manner on the treatment of prisoners of war by the Serb authorities and on the conditions in prisons in those municipalities where such cases exist. They're to do this through the municipal bodies of Internal Affairs and administrations of penal/correctional facilities respectively. Now, first thing, Mr. Mandic, do you remember getting an order that a report should be produced or official written information?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And given what you've been asserting all the way through, that everything to do with virtually 95 per cent of prisoners was to do with military, why was it that the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Justice were being ordered to obtain official information rather than the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, through intelligence, the police would compile reports and present a realistic and objective picture of the situation in the municipal prisons to the president of the country. It was not the army who should do that. It was up to the police. As far as the minister of judiciary was concerned in penal and correctional facilities, non-Serbs were held that had been captured by the army. They were decided, their fate was decided by the army; however, while they were in prison, it was the ministry of judiciary that took care of them. It sounds a bit complicated. It probably requires some clarification. For example, in Sarajevo now, in the penal and correctional facility Butmir, there are persons incarcerated by the cantonal court, the Sarajevo court, or any other court from Bosnia-Herzegovina, irrespective of whether they are being investigated or serving the sentence. So they were incarcerated by those institutions that tried them. But they are all centralised, they are kept on the same location, and they were guarded by the police of Republika Srpska, but the BH ministry, relevant ministry, was responsible for them. However, if there is an ongoing investigation, it's the BH court or the competent court of Republika Srpska or the Federation is in charge. This is why the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina is somewhat complex and complicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, let's not concern ourselves about what's happening in modern day Sarajevo. But here, what is actually being -- you're -- being asked you of is on the treatment of prisoners of war, not civilians or -- or criminals, but prisoners of war, which, as you know, Mr. Mandic, as a lawyer, has a legally defined definition.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat, concerning POWs or the civilians, it was the army who was responsible to decide their fate, whether they would be kept or released. However, as for the situation within the prisons, it was the Ministry of Justice that was responsible for them why they are being incarcerated. If the army took them out to perform labour or transfer them to a different location, it was their responsibility, the army's responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be marked and admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In light of that answer that you have just given us, Mr. Mandic, can I just ask you to look at another document. It's actually 10318 at tab 91. It's not on our 65 ter list, but I think I better ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Yes, I crossed it through because ... I don't know whether we can get it up. No, I'm sorry, Your Honour. What happened was that I went through removing it, because I didn't think it was relevant either. But it was on the original list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Apologies to the counsel while we are waiting. The last exhibit number is P1330.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, well, I gather I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands. It was originally on our list, but it wasn't on our 65 ter, so we removed it. But it's directly on point. Well, all right. Listen, I'll move on, Your Honours, I can come back to it, if necessary. Can we look, then, please, next at -- yes, tab 100. Sorry - tab 100 - 1214, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, again, this is the -- a government session held in September. You were there, Mr. Mandic. It was held on the 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go, please, to the fifth page. And it's Agenda item 20. Fifth page in English and sixth page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, a delegation was being formed comprising, Mr. Djeric, Mr. Trbojevic, Mr. Pejic, yourself, Mico Stanisic, Mr. Subotic, Colonel Subotic, and somebody called Petra Markovic who are to attend the meeting, Bijelina, on the 12th of September this year, scheduled by representatives from the Krajina and Posavina areas. This was, as we will see, a few days before an Assembly meeting took place in Bijeljina. What was to be discussed at this meeting that involved such a high-level delegation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Because you did attend --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there perhaps a conclusion somewhere in the minutes, to refresh my memory? I can't remember otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think we'll see it is referred to in the Assembly that took place. Let's move straight to that, please, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I have this one. I don't think this document has been admitted yet. Has it? I'll just check. No, it hasn't. Can this be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1331, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now let's go to -- immediately to the Assembly session on the 14th and 5th of September, which is P430.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can we have a tab number, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab -- I'm sorry, 98.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we'll see in a moment you were there again because the question of the judges was raised, or at least two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go, please, to page 8 in English, and to page 7 in the B/C/S. No, you've gone on page 5 in B/C/S. 7, please. Two pages on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you there, didn't you, proposed that the two Montenegrin judges, not the others, but the two Montenegrins, should be placed on -- their election should be placed on the agenda. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we move on to -- just a moment. Let me get the right page. Yes. There's a long discussion. You speak again, but let's just have a look at what happens so we don't waste time. Hmm, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think if we go to page 115 in the English. And to 100 -- and to 37 in B/C/S. No, sorry, there's two pages. All right. I have forgotten, it splits in the middle of this. The number at the top is 0422-6316. Thank you. I'm not sure who -- I think, yes, Dr. Milanovic, I think, is speaking. I'm not sure who is. "I just want to say I'm not an extremist or anything, but Mr. Kupresanin is right. We are being deceived. "This man cannot be the deputy public prosecutor [indiscernible] -- soldiers and our heroes because he might try them as war criminals in future. Number 5 on the list cannot pass; Ibrahim Alagic, son of Adem. He must have taken part in the prosecution of Serbs ten years ago. And then you, Mr. Mandic, explain the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, if we go on, please, to page 117 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters would kindly ask Mrs. Prosecutor to indicate which paragraph she is reading from. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I do my best. It's quite difficult to -- right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric -- and I'm afraid that I'm not sure whether it should be -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm sorry because I've made -- I think I have rather made a mess of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mandic, at this meeting, do you remember Mr. Djuric saying again: "In respect of these appointments, if our representatives need to show Europe three Muslims or two Croats, I'm all for it," in respect of election of judges and prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I can't find the part in B/C/S, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I'm just going to ask you if you recall that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I suggested that it be included in the agenda again to elect prosecutors and judges of different ethnicities. And again MPs contested it; some MPs contested it, including Djuric. That was a problem in the parliament. That's what we discussed some time ago. Nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we'll have to leave that because, as I say, it's rather too lengthy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we please now move to number 99 -- sorry, 65 ter 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a bulletin. Again, we're back to Vogosca. And apparently two prisoner, Muslims it would appear, on the 24th of September, 1992, were hit because they were carrying out works. As the minister of justice, would you expect to be informed if prisoners were killed whilst they were being made to work?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Madam Prosecutor, that it's a section of the prison in the Serbian Municipality of Vogosca. You -- you don't see any reference to the Ministry of Justice. It has nothing to do with the prison which was within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice. And I was precisely saying that we, in the government, established a commission to disband these municipal prisons. This says Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbian Municipality of Vogosca, Prison Department. It doesn't say penal correctional facility. This is exactly the kind of prison that we abolished because they were irregular and illegal and they were under the authority of the army, because they were established by the army and the Crisis Staffs. It's the same thing I was talking about before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but the document that exactly we saw saying that all these, as it were, rough and ready prisons should be abolished and brought within the penal/correction system was some four months, if not longer, before this. Had any further steps been taken to deal with these prisons?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. For instance, in Vogosca, Hadzici, and Ilijas, there were at least five or six of those centres detaining non-Serbs, before this date, and this was run by the army. And that's the military prison in Vogosca -- or, rather, Planja's House as it was called, within which there was a section for the court in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I can clarify the answer, 67, line 24. I believe the witness said that these five or six centres were closed before this date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's completely different. That's not the interpretation we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is why I want -- that is what I heard the witness said, and I would like you to -- to explore that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, rather than telling him ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm really sorry because I don't have my earphones on. I'm listening to the witness. And that is what I heard. And everybody can confirm that who speaks Serbian in the audience.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you heard all that, Mr. Mandic, no doubt. Is that what you said, that they were closed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that in the meantime the prison called Punkir [phoen] was closed down and then the Sonja, Trvan [phoen], and some others run by the municipal authorities in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but clearly some were still operating, as you say, including Planja's House, which you knew about.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Planja's House was a military prison run by the army. And within that prison there was a section that was within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice. In fact, the remand prison of the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This one, however, you say, or this, relates entirely to an illegal type of detention facility, as I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for this prison section, if people were kept there without any charges and any proceedings against them, of course, that was illegal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you knew these prisons were carrying on and you say they were all to do with the army, did you, at any stage, in your position as minister, complain to Dr. Karadzic or complain to General Mladic or anyone that there were these prisons being run by the military in which civilians were being detained, in which people were being killed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And to whom did you complain?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before this last break, we looked at one letter that I sent for the second time to Mr. Karadzic in which I asked that the military prosecution and the judiciary be integrated with the civilian prosecution and judiciary to prevent further illegal detention of such people in those prisons. We in the Ministry of Justice had no jurisdiction over these detained non-Serbs. And that's why I resigned in November, I think just before the session of the -- the Assembly held in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In February.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the military prosecution and judiciary were so busy and we had no power over anything and nothing to do, because the state of immediate threat of war had been proclaimed. We were looking at that letter I wrote just recently, a letter I sent to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Mandic, but you don't in that letter - and we can go back to it if you like - I don't in that letter say "because there are people being illegally detained and being killed." You say that the courts aren't operating properly. And we can go back to it if we need to.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one consequence of that is the failure of the military prosecution to operate. Because if they were working properly, people would not have been illegally detained in prisons. It needed a systemic solution to ensure that all the work is lawful. The problem was a systemic one; it was not about individual cases. I raised that issue at several Assembly sessions in Zvornik, for instance, in September. There was a discussion between me and General Gvero about the operation of the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner. 70, 13, it's recorded September, and I believe the witness said the Assembly in Zvornik and the different -- a different month.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it was corrected to say February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. It says, page 70, line 13, I raised the issue --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. What date do you say that was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was November 1992 in Zvornik, and September in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I think the best I can do with this is ask for this document to be marked for identification at the moment. Document 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked pending what? Where do you see the Prosecution going with this, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I rather think that -- you mean can I find another witness to do deal with it? I don't know. But I rather think it's quite important that two prisoners, Muslims, are sent off to do work as a result of which they're killed. And Vogosca is one of the indictment -- one of the municipalities in our indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is -- is there a Defence objection to this document being marked or even admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We do not object to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1332, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just ask, somewhat impertinently, but is Your Honours' hesitation on the basis you don't see the relevance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No. Actually I was wondering whether the -- having regard to your explanation, whether the document -- when it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, I would like it admitted, but I didn't think I could because Mr. Mandic says he doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It certainly meets the threshold, in my view, for being marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Slightly concerned, that's all. Right, yes. I don't think I can deal with that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, could I ask you to look, please, at document 1738, please. Very quickly, Mr. Mandic, this is headed an overview of courts and judges in the prosecutor's office. Is this, as far as you're concerned, an accurate document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't think we need to go further, particularly given the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1333, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, can we look, please, next at document 259. This document, dated the 22nd of October, 1992, addressed to General Mladic, Mr. Stanisic, and yourself, from Mr. Karadzic. And it -- he is saying that local police, military, and civilian authorities are completely disregarding his authorisation that the ICRC should be allowed to visit prisons and that you were to worn your subordinated officers. Were you aware that the ICRC was being refused admittance to prisons under the control of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international representatives were never, ever prevented from going into prisons controlled by the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, when you got this letter, did you approach Dr. Karadzic and say, We've never prevented the ICRC from going in?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic wrote here that police and civilian authorities were concerned, municipal authorities. However, I forwarded these letters to -- to the penal/correctional facilities, repeating instructions that they should keep to the rules of the service. There was no problem in these prisons in admitting the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you didn't answer -- I'm sorry. The question I asked, Mr. Mandic, was did you say to Dr. Karadzic, As far as the Ministry of Justice is concerned and the penal facilities that come under its jurisdiction, there is no problem?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I informed him or not. But I certainly now that there was no problem there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we simply have it marked and admitted, please. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1334, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with Mico Stanisic what his police were doing in respect of prisoners, while we're on that topic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the police held any prisoners at this time or that they ran prisons. There were only prisons run by the Ministry of Justice and prisons controlled by the military prosecutor's office or, rather, the army. I don't think that the police ran any prisons. At least I'm not aware of that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at the letter that you wrote at this period, please, which is document, please, 381. Or that went out under your signature, under your stamp. Letter from you addressed to the Serbian municipalities of Hadzici and Ilidza, to the president of the -- and the chief of the public security station personally. The investigation of this ministry showed that on the territory of your respective municipalities, in the facilities of the sport centre in Hadzici, there are 90 detained persons of Muslim ethnicity, and in Ilidza, in the facilities of the high school for graphic education, about 30 persons. And you should transfer the above mentioned to Butmir. And, at the same time, we are informing you our investigation extensive as well as observation by the International Red Cross and United Nation -- regarding the breaches committed regarding the liberation of the persons of Muslim ethnicity. And there's a signature, your name, and a stamp. So, first of all, Mr. Mandic, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not my signature or the number of the protocol 04/2. My number was 01. I don't know who this -- it's Slobodan Avlijas actually who did the inspection. He is not from my office. But he made this inquiry and he wrote to Ilidza and Hadzici to correct these irregularities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The answer was not recorded as I heard it. Because the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's -- let's before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I just wanted to point out. I'm not saying what I heard. He -- he was pointing out that he knew who -- that he knows the person who signed this document. That was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh I see. He said that he did, yes. Sorry, I had that. Sorry that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This document was signed by Mr. Avlijas wasn't it whom you did know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was an assistant in my ministry. And in the top left corner 04/2 that is his department, his administration. And he falsified my signature. Because he is the one who made the inquiry in Hadzici and Ilidza municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But he came under you as a minister, didn't he? He was responsible to you as the minister.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you just told us not a minute ago that there were no -- firstly there was no problem with the ICRC; and, secondly, you were unaware of any detention facilities which were being run by the police.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know at the time that the police ran prisons. The person who inspected and checked this was Slobodan Avlijas. You can call him to appear here as a witness and ask him to explain this. I honestly never, at the time, knew about the police running any prisons. I knew that it was done by the army and the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wasn't Mr. Avlijas who was doing these inspections duty-bound to give you a report about what he had found?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, that he sent this on behalf of the ministry with his protocol number and my signature. My block signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- are you saying that he signed this or that he forged your name, your signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He falsified my signature. You say -- see it says M. Mandic. It is though similar to my signature but one can see it's not the same and identical. And he put his number 04/2. My number was 1/2 and then all the other deputies were 3 and 4 and other numbers. Every department had their own protocol number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, wouldn't Mr. Avlijas have been taking a risk first in not telling you about what he had found, and secondly, in forging your signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't answer this. He's the one who can answer that. But this is definitely a forgery, and this is definitely his protocol number, and it was him who definitely inspected these areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you think of any reason why he wouldn't have told you what he had found?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't. I saw this letter in the BH court in Sarajevo and it was established there, positively established, that this is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can contact him. He is an available, and can he be called up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1335, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You are about to make an objection, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honours, but you were faster than my objection. Well, I believe that the witness said that -- that -- that his signature was forged. I don't -- I really have a problem if we -- if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I heard everything the witness said. It -- it -- it -- it strikes me that the -- a lot of the exchange between Ms. Korner and the witness over the past ten minutes really has to do with the -- well, did not -- as I understand the witness's testimony, result in his denying the authenticity of the contents of the document, notwithstanding the irregularities - my word - in the way that it was produced, and the -- his non-acceptance of the purported signature of him notwithstanding the fact that he was a minister on it. So taking all of that into consideration, the document by itself, on its face, I would have thought would be admissible, but I anticipate the -- that the -- when the time comes the -- to the extent that this is relevant to the Defence case, there would be arguments about what weight to be attached to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I'm grateful to Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Ms. Korner, you are within the last eight minutes of you're allotted time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In that case, can we move --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just have a minute, Your Honours, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to do with municipalities and municipal Crisis Staffs that had set up illegal prisons, not the police. So it was the municipalities who, through their Crisis Staffs and Territorial Defence, set up these institutions. So this was not a falsified development, event but there is no information, actually I don't have any information that this refers to the police. This had to do with the municipalities and their Crisis Staffs. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then very quickly, Mr. Mandic, because you heard my time is running out. Could you have a look, please, at document 0 -- 258 -- oh, sorry, no, P393, MFI'd. And it's tab 109. This report on prisons and collection camps addressed to the President, or the Presidency, Dr. Karadzic, President of the Republika Srpska, chairman of the Assembly, and prime minister of the Republika Srpska. It has got a signature on it? Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is again a forgery done by Slobodan Avlijas. It is his protocol number. However, I am familiar with this report and the report is true. This is just for the sake of the truth that I wanted to say this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to come on to that. Because there went up to --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this it says 04/2, and the signature which is similar to mine but it's not mine. But I am familiar with the contents of this report, and I ordered it to be sent out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I don't want to waste too much time on this, but this is a report that you were ordered to do, which you sent, and -- just a moment let me finish. And on this occasion you know all about this report. You see it. But Mr. Avlijas forges your signature? Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He signed this just for the sake of -- of expeditiousness. But I was familiarised with the content, and I insisted on this report being sent out immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And are you sure, the last document about which we've had so much discussion that wasn't signed for him for expeditious -- expedition on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was sent to two or three municipalities. He ordered on my behalf of these municipal prisons to be shut down, and the report that we saw earlier was incorporated into this comprehensive report which was sent to the President of the Republic, the parliament, Speaker, and the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, just let's briefly just look at a couple of the entries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For Prijedor, number 4, page 5. It's page 3 in the B/C/S. No, okay. Sorry -- sorry, page 4, not page 5. Page 4. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Prijedor, neither a camp nor a prison for prisoners of war officially exists in Prijedor. Former collection centre at Trnopolje was closed down by agreement. This report is 22nd of October. However, because of irresponsible people in Prijedor launched the misinformation amongst the Muslim population that the only way to leave this town for the desired destination is to gather at the Trnopolje centre, and so on and so forth. Where did this information come from?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government had set up a commission and the commission was sent out into the field. Some people went to Krajina, some went to Herzegovina, some to Central Bosnia, some went to northern Bosnia. So it is a complication an aggregate report that was drafted and sent out to all the competent institutions in order to inform them about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the situation on the ground, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, I'm sorry, you sent people out to gather information from the various municipalities. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No it wasn't me. It was the decision taken by the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But then -- all right. Well let's just move to Sanski Most, number 5. So -- no, stay on the B/C/S and go to -- one further page on in English. Information that there was camp in Sanski Most is not correct. In that area only four people were taken to prisoner and transferred to Manjaca camp during combat activities. Did you realise from your own sources of information as a member of the government during the period of April to July 1992 that that was completely false?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information relating to Sanski Most and Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all that I'm going to ask you about that report. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number will remain Exhibit P393, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was MFI'd before; that's why. Yes, Your Honours, I think, in fact, because the November -- it -- in -- well, perhaps can I deal with this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just very quickly. In November, at the Assembly meeting, Mr. Djeric, did he not, Djeric, made various allegations in respect of you and Mr. Stanisic's work; is that right? And both of you responded to it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think -- perhaps I can just ask you about a couple of things that Mr. Stanisic said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, then, at P400. And in the English, it's at page 19; and in the B/C/S, it's at page 14. Or it begins at page 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see Mr. Stanisic spoke. Mr. Mandic, you'd spoken, first of all, and then Mr. Stanisic spoke. And could we go, please, one page further in English and B/C/S. Mr. Stanisic said that -- thank you very much. Referring to what Mr. Djeric asked for. I emphasise here in front of you that I followed a policy of the Presidency of the Serbian Democratic Party and our deputies in the former state, and I have always been in favour of that policy. Did you take the same line as -- [indiscernible] did you feel the same way as Mr. Stanisic that what had you done was follow the policy of the Presidency of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, yes. That's what Mr. Stanisic said. And I'm asking if your view, what you had done, the actions had you taken during the period between March and November 1992 was to follow the policy of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please explain to me what actions you're referring to? All we did was implement the laws adopted by the Assembly. I don't know which particular actions you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The actions that you took, in respect of what happened in March, and April, your involvement with the police, your work as minister of justice, and those who were prisoners, was that the actions -- were the actions you took those that were the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party was. I wasn't a member of that political party. Throughout the whole of my life and particularly during that period, I always worked and complied with the law. I worked according to my conscience and my belief that I was doing the best I could. I didn't follow anyone's policy. I did not follow any political party, including the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just ask you then about one other thing that Mr. Stanisic said in respect of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we look at page 21 -- well, the next page in English, and I think it's the next page also in B/C/S. And it's -- if we could highlight the last paragraph in each.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic said there: "We had to take criminals and crooks because, you know, that no intellectual took the rifle in his hand and went to fight for the country." You were for at least nearly two months a minister of the MUP, assistant minister. Was that something that you realised, that criminals and crooks had been taken into the police force?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never had criminals and crooks been engaged by the service. And he was not referring to the police at all. No one could join the police who had criminal record. But Mr. Stanisic was making a totally different reference. This was taken out of context. And I categorically assert that not a single person with criminal past and a police record was admitted into police, and I can say that before this Honourable Chamber because I know that for a fact. That was never done. For sure. At least while I was in the police, but I also don't think that Mico Stanisic had allowed that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you say I took this out of context --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence. That was the reason why the joint MUP broke up, because hundreds of Muslim criminals joined them from abroad. That's why we had these meetings in Sarajevo where we pointed out to Minister Delimustafic that criminals with criminal records were putting on police uniforms. That caused the disintegration of the police. And that Bihavija [phoen], from the Shiite police, were joining the MUP. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that -- perhaps we ought to look -- go back a bit. Because the paragraph starts -- well, not starts: I must also warn you this state has been built out of chaos, no law regulations. You all know that the police have built this country from the beginning, along with the people, defending them and providing space for the government to make law regulations, and so on and so forth. I'm always ready to present to you all that we have done during that period. There were no regulations. Intentions were good. But if there were any mistakes, we are ready to discuss them and to answer for them. Therefore, I do not agree that anyone can, say, call someone to be Radovan's man based on that -- and based on that to claim is he no good. We also have to take criminals and crooks, et cetera. So he was talking about the police, wasn't he, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just briefly say the following --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. If this is going to affect the witness's testimony, then he ought to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's not going to affect the witness's testimony. I'm just wondering what is the purpose of this exercise? Namely, Your Honours, my client --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I'm -- Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If this is -- this -- this should not be done in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going into the specific facts at all. I'm just stating --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the situation as it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I object, Your Honour. If there's going to be any statement made about Mr. Stanisic is or was or what's going happen should not happen in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine with me. Witness can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would it be sufficient for the witness to remove his headphones? He speaks English. Yes, well, it's time for today's adjournment in any event. It seems that this is a matter that we would have to continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just sa one sentence, Your Honours? Stanisic said here, They took on board crooks and criminals. "They," not "I." He wasn't speaking about himself, about the ministry, or police. He was speaking in general terms. And we shall see who was it who engaged and recruited criminals and crooks when we come to that, who insisted on them being brought into Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were notes, shorthand notes, about that. He said "they," and he was referring to powerful people who were able to bring people from other countries to kill and loot throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was not a reference to the police or to the Minister Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. That seems to be a suitable dramatic note on which to take the adjournment until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of May, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
